legacy_conversion_note: Original source (source/Y3/Session 4/Carpenter/Case Study_ Carpenter.docx + Guide Notes.docx). The protagonist (Newt Harrison, carpenter), the clients (Spencer and Michelle Berisel, downtown Montreal Airbnb flat, comfort-and-luxury goal), the CD$17,900 soft flooring budget cap, the Burlington VT cross-border materials sourcing with its 2.6% delivery fee, and the three-material dilemma (carpet, hardwood, tile) are preserved verbatim from the source. The third option offered in the original (tile throughout) was dropped per project-owner review (cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md) as the weakest fit, leaving a clean binary carpet-vs-hardwood dilemma (kitchen/bathrooms are tiled either way, unchanged). The source docx's own material/maintenance cost table was NOT reused verbatim -- it carried no citations and its figures could not be verified as real -- and was fully replaced with current 2026 U.S. flooring-cost data, publicly verifiable via the sources[] entries below (Homewyse, HomeGuide, NAHB/Bank of America, Bank of Canada). The source's floor-plan appendix image (House Plan Europe.jpeg, a generic stock 3-bedroom floor plan, not a real photograph of the Berisels' actual flat) is preserved as the geometric basis for Appendix A's room-by-room takeoff, with its meter dimensions reproduced and converted to square feet -- this is declared as Modeling Assumption MA1 (case.md Appendix F), not presented as a real, externally-verifiable property record. The original Guide Notes.docx content did not actually describe this case (it was a mismatched/reused template about a different family's flooding-and-inheritance scenario, with unrelated stock images) and was not usable; FACILITATOR.md's anchor ladder, twist, Socratic questions, and cohort bands are newly authored for Carpenter specifically, following this project's current 11-anchor structure.

deliverables.text: A room-by-room area takeoff converting the floor plan's metric dimensions into square feet, ending in two zone totals (carpet/hardwood zone; tile zone).

A materials-and-delivery worksheet per option: material cost, 2.6% delivery fee, installation labor, converted USD to CAD at the current exchange rate, ending in one total initial cost per option in CAD.
A total initial cost comparison against the CD$17,900 soft budget cap, stating how far each option sits above or below it.
A cumulative cost-over-time chart at the 5/10/15-year marks for each option, as a line or bar graph.
A percent-difference calculation stating how close Option A's and Option B's 15-year total costs of ownership come to each other.

balance.argument_a: Option A (carpet) has a much lower initial cost -- CD$14,640.92 vs. Option B's CD$22,805.26, roughly CD$8,164 cheaper up front -- and it is the only option that fits under the Berisels' CD$17,900 soft budget cap by a comfortable margin (18.2% under), while Option B blows past the cap by 27.4%. Read the ordinary residential wear-life figures from Appendix B at face value, and Option A also wins on 15-year total cost of ownership -- by a razor-thin 2.8%.
balance.argument_b: Option B (hardwood) matches the Berisels' own stated 'comfort and luxury' goal directly, and its wear-life advantage is not just longer -- it survives real Airbnb-style heavy, weekly-turnover foot traffic in a way carpet's much shorter cited wear life does not. Once that traffic pattern is factored into how often carpet actually needs full replacement inside the 15-year horizon (not the generic residential figure Appendix B cites), hardwood's 15-year total cost of ownership overtakes carpet's and becomes the cheaper option, by 15.3%.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric = 15-year total cost of ownership (CAD): initial install (materials + 2.6% delivery + labor, USD->CAD at 1.3785) plus all maintenance/replacement over 15 years. Base reading (Appendix B/C figures applied at face value, one carpet replacement at year 10; hardwood serviced only at the two years Appendix F MA3 actually states -- recoat year 5, refinish year 10): Option A = CD$33,723.93, Option B = CD$34,674.14, margin = (34674.14-33723.93)/33723.93 = 2.8%, Option A cheaper. Twist reading (short-term-rental heavy traffic roughly halves carpet's effective replacement trigger, forcing two full carpet replacements -- year 5 and year 10 -- inside the 15-year horizon instead of one; hardwood's schedule is unaffected): Option A = CD$39,986.87, Option B = CD$34,674.14, margin = (39986.87-34674.14)/34674.14 = 15.3%, Option B cheaper. The twist flips the winner. See sensitivity_model.py evaluate()/evaluate_twist(). (Corrected 2026-08-20 after Tier 2 probe 1 cold-solve caught an undocumented third hardwood service event in an earlier model version -- see sensitivity_model.py's CORRECTION note.)

modeling_assumptions.text: Room dimensions and square footage, adapted from a real published floor plan of comparable size, meters converted to square feet.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The carpet/hardwood zone's square footage scales the cost gap between options directly.

modeling_assumptions.text: Carpet wear-life trigger set at the upper end (10 yrs) of the sourced 8-10 year range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Using the lower end changes replacement-event count within the 15-year horizon.

modeling_assumptions.text: Hardwood recoat/refinish schedule fixed at year 5 (recoat) and year 10 (full refinish).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: A different schedule inside the cited ranges shifts timing, not total 15-year magnitude.

modeling_assumptions.text: Whether short-term-rental (weekly-turnover) foot traffic changes wear-life/maintenance schedules from Appendix B/C's general residential figures.
modeling_assumptions.value: Not applied in the base pitch; applied in the Twist
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the case's single most load-bearing assumption -- it flips the winner.

sensitivity_note: Base reading (residential wear-life figures at face value): Option A wins 15-year TCO by 2.8% -- a razor-thin margin. Applying short-term-rental heavy-traffic wear (the Twist) to carpet's replacement cadence flips the winner to Option B by 15.3%. See sensitivity_model.py.

sensitivity_disclosure.effect: Scales both options' cost gap roughly proportionally; does not flip the base-reading winner at the tested range.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: How long carpet actually survives in this specific fictional short-term rental before a full replacement is genuinely bought cannot be known in advance by research -- it depends on future guest behavior, maintenance quality, and traffic that has not happened yet, the same kind of irreducible forecast uncertainty as a future price. MA2 fixes the case at the sourced range's upper end (10 years); at -50% (5 years) the verdict flips to A, and at +50% (15 years) the margin widens past the SPEC §2 20% cap. Both directions are disclosed here and in FACILITATOR.md/case.md's Modeling Assumptions, not hidden. Given the base margin is already only 2.8%, this dial is doing real work -- flagged as the case's single most load-bearing sensitivity alongside MA4.
